entities.name: Jan de Bakker
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Jansz de Bakker van Woerden (c. 1499 – September 15, 1525) stands as the inaugural Roman Catholic priest in the Northern Netherlands to suffer execution specifically for his emerging Protestant convictions, marking a pivotal moment in the nascent Dutch Reformation. His public burning at the stake in The Hague, ordered by the local Inquisition and civil authorities, solidified him as an early martyr for the Reformed cause, challenging the entrenched power of the Catholic Church and the Holy Roman Empire under Charles V. De Bakker's fate illuminated the brutal realities of religious persecution gripping Europe in the wake of Martin Luther's theses, transforming a local cleric into a symbol of resistance against ecclesiastical dogma and imperial decree.

Born in Woerden, Jan de Bakker initially followed his father, Jan de Bakker senior, into the priestly vocation, studying in Leuven and possibly Wittenberg, where he likely encountered Lutheran ideas directly. Upon returning to Woerden, he began openly preaching doctrines considered heretical by the Catholic Church, including the rejection of transubstantiation, the celibacy of priests, and the necessity of good works for salvation, advocating for justification by faith alone. His reformist sermons quickly drew the attention of the ecclesiastical authorities. After a period of imprisonment in Brussels in 1523, from which he escaped, de Bakker was re-arrested in The Hague in May 1525, where he faced a tribunal led by the Inquisitor Jacob van Hoogstraten.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jan de Bakker's execution as the first priest-martyr for Protestant beliefs in the Northern Netherlands galvanized the nascent Dutch Reformation, providing a powerful symbol of resistance against Catholic persecution. His unwavering defiance and subsequent commemoration in martyrologies profoundly shaped the collective identity and historical narrative of Dutch Protestantism.
